title: Biventricular arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy diagnosed in a young patient: A case report with literature review
case_prompt:
An 18-year-old man with no personal or family history presented in 2021 with chest pain. Physical examination was unremarkable. ECG showed an incomplete right bundle-branch block and negative T waves in the inferolateral leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed apical akinesia of the left ventricle with a preserved ejection fraction of 55%. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with late gadolinium enhancement demonstrated subepicardial contrast uptake in the apex and apical segments of the anterolateral and inferior LV walls; the right ventricle appeared normal. A diagnosis of myocarditis was made on the basis of myocardial fibrosis, and the patient was prescribed a β-blocker, with poor compliance.

One year later, during a football match, he experienced exertional syncope. ECG now showed repolarization abnormalities. Troponin and brain natriuretic peptide levels were elevated. Repeat cardiac MRI revealed akinesia of the LV apex extending to the apical and mid segments of adjacent walls, with a mildly reduced LV ejection fraction of 45%, and akinesia of the inferior RV wall. Late gadolinium enhancement was transmural in the apex and in the apical and mid segments of the inferior, anterior, septal, and lateral LV walls, with enhancement of the inferior and lateral RV walls. Two diagnoses were considered: necrotic sequela versus arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. To rule out ischemic necrosis, coronary angiography was performed and found to be normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Myocarditis was initially considered on the basis of LV subepicardial fibrosis — “The diagnosis retained was myocarditis due the presence of foci of myocardial fibrosis.”  
2. Ischemic necrosis from myocardial infarction was considered given the transmural enhancement but was excluded after normal coronary arteries — “To rule out the first diagnosis, the patient underwent coronary angiography which was normal.”  
3. Biventricular arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy was diagnosed phenotypically using imaging and ECG criteria in the absence of genetic testing — “The diagnosis of biventricular ACM was retained based on Padua Criteria.”
